As of writing this, Grave of the Fireflies is the #1 highest rated standalone anime movie on Letterboxd, and it boggles the mind that they achieved such a feat because this is one of the worst movies I have ever seen. I generally have a hatred for Studio Ghibli but even among the ones I have seen, this is still the worst. All characters, including protagonists, are generally emotionless, hollow, and unlikeable. Early on, their mother dies and her body is brutally scarred by the flames. This could have led to a sympathetic moment for our protagonist when he comes face-to-face with her, but instead he feels literally nothing about seeing his mother’s charred body. The ending about how the main characters die is openly spoiled at the very beginning of the movie, so there’s no hope or suspense for them that gets tragically ripped away from you. Dramatic music is played at bizarre moments almost as if you’re supposed to be feeling something that resonates in your heart but instead you’re just bored and waiting for something compelling to happen. I am a very easy person to make cry while watching something, and this movie is often praised as a heart-rending tearjerker. However, I spent the whole duration either with a stone-cold poker face or laughing at how bad this movie is.

On a purely technical level, Grave of the Fireflies is a well-crafted piece of cinema. The animation is beautiful, the pacing flows without major structural gaps, and it certainly doesn't pull its punches. But as a narrative experience, it is a deeply frustrating work that mistakes emotional manipulation for profound storytelling. It is a movie that relies entirely on a rigged script and a manufactured world of selective psychopathy, ultimately earning a 1/10 rather than the masterpiece status it is often granted. The film’s biggest narrative failure is its structure. By spoiling Seita’s death in the very first scene, the movie robs itself of any actual plot progression or suspense. The runtime becomes a clinical countdown to an inevitable tragedy. You don’t leave the movie heartbroken because you went on a deeply complex journey with these specific characters; you leave feeling miserable simply because you just watched an adorable four-year-old bottle of sugar slowly starve to death and drink her own blood in a dirt hole. The film relies on the basic biological reflex that seeing a toddler suffer is inherently sad, using Setsuko’s innocence as a weapon to force tears out of the audience rather than earning them through a compelling, organic script. Worse still is the blatant logical contradiction in the world the film builds. The script explicitly goes out of its way to show that Japan’s wartime society is still highly organized: banks are open for Seita to withdraw a fortune, police stations are running, trains are functional, and rationing systems are strictly managed. Yet, in a society that heavily bureaucratic, the script requires every adult to catch a sudden case of collective, selective psychopathy. The aunt is the ultimate embodiment of this artificial cruelty. Her expectations of Seita are completely unhinged, demanding that a fourteen-year-old middle schooler find a job as a steelworker in an active war zone where bombs are dropping daily. When she forces them out, the rest of the family—her husband and daughter living in that exact same house—apparently never once asks where their dead relative's orphaned children went. To believe this story, you have to believe that an entire community completely turned off the "human brain" switch, ignoring a teenager and a toddler rotting in a nearby dirt hole. This isn't a realistic depiction of societal breakdown under stress; it is a narrative corridor that selectively deletes basic human curiosity and family logic just to ensure a child dies for the plot. The only adults granted an ounce of honor or discipline are the military personnel, which veers the film dangerously close to historical propaganda. By positioning ordinary civilian citizens as the heartless villains, the movie subtly sanitizes the military's role in the war, focusing entirely on how much the nation suffered rather than why they were in that war to begin with. Grave of the Fireflies functions perfectly if its only goal is to make you feel bad for ninety minutes. But because it breaks its own internal logic and overrides natural human empathy just to force a predetermined, manipulative ending, it remains a hollow watch. It is a well-made emotional torture device that you will never need to see again.

maybe it’s because im jaded after reading stuff like the tin drum, but this movie is hollow for me. i understand it’s a localized narrative about two siblings and in that regard the movie is fine and sad, but i think its impossible to isolate the wider sociopolitical context of this movie from the siblings journey. japan has, uniquely, continued to systemically downplay its actions during the second world war, from school textbook revisions that caused outcry from okinawa natives in 2007 to state visits honoring class a war criminals in the yasukuni shrine. what is the relevance of this to this movie? well, i think it rings hollow to depict this story without addressing the genocidal machine that fueled it. yes, the director has stated, “it is not at all an anti-war anime and contains absolutely no such message", but maybe it should? the kneejerk response to this sentiment is always “well the civilians getting bombed weren’t the IJA committing crimes in china”, which is true, and rings true for germans as well. however, it is a fact that vergangenheitsbewältigung, or ‘work of historical coping’, has been a literary and social effort in the wider conscious of germany in the journey of confronting the crimes of their state and people. unlike günter grass, it always seems to me that japanese authors and directors refuse to challenge or address the political themes and historical facts of the second world war that led to the circumstances they wish to depict in victimizing tones. maybe im wrong and there is a movement to address this to a wider scale than I understand, but that’s my impression on many of these kind of films, including wind rises. even seita isn’t innocent, but it’s not like they’ll address why he has to make the decisions he does, because that would require talking about politics. overall, I think the pacifist message of this movie and others like it doesn’t really work when you refuse to address why that pacifism is so socially desired in this historical moment. the siblings story doesn’t exist in a vacuum and is only happening because their father and his compatriots are waging a war of genocidal conquest. at least oskar matzeraths father choked to death on his nazi party pin.

First watched a couple of years ago, many of the images seen now incapable of being unseen, scorched deep into my mind. NONETHELESS, Grave of the fireflies is not much more than a hefty dollop of misery porn to choke on; nothing new here, nothing much to say - a tediously simple film. The animation is beautiful as expected, even despite being hollowed out by a narrative devoid of tension following a ruleset dead set on placing your tear ducts under considerable strain without ever once demonstrating interest in venturing into territories beyond surface level "human" suffering. I am slightly surprised - and certainly more offended - that Grave of the Fireflies is nearly on par with Spirited Away in terms of critical reception, at least as demonstrated by y’all folks here on letterboxd: Whereas one film is a incredible example in world-building teeming with ideas miraculously materialised into concrete shapes and forms, evoking an extensive palette of emotions, this film is simply a generic rehash of “the strife of children during times of war” repackaged in the form of a simplistically monotone studio Ghibli film. When will we learn that heavy emotional provocation does not always equate to a “good” film? When will we no longer uphold studios or directors as gods incapable of slipping into the territory of what is often dubbed as “mediocrity”? Alas… All hail Studio Ghibli supremacy! Poor children though, of course.

There's a lot of mysticism around this film, and all the noise about how heartbreaking it is put me off from watching it for a very long time. Now that I have watched it, I feel a bit underwhelmed and confused. The movie is not an anti-war movie; not only has this been confirmed by the director, but the overall story is not too interested in the war itself. We sometimes see the attacks, but only one casualty that is relevant is caused directly by the war. Of course, the little girl would not have died in peaceful times, but the survival of the two kids is only created from the lack of empathy and humanity that a war-torn society demonstrates. The boy was more offended at Imperial Japan losing the war than her own family treating him and his sister like burdens. In 2026 it is very easy to see the first scenes and think about Palestine, Iran, Lebanon, and all these countries that have been attacked by the USA and Israel, but as the movie continues, you wonder more and more how the story was actually created: Japan at that time was an imperial force, engaging in violence to further expand its geographical and political dominance. If I first saw the burnt corpses and thought of the very graphic images coming from Gaza, I then realized that I wouldn't have a similar reaction to the image of an Israeli soldier in the same position. But that is part of the issue, I think. The main theme of the movie is not war or how war destroys lives and everything we find normal. No, the theme is how war makes us less human. A crying child who misses her mother—a mother who is dead but she doesn't know it yet—is more disruptive than the alarms that announce upcoming attacks. Sharing a bowl of white rice with family goes from being a happy memory to a reason for resentment. It is a bit shallow, in my opinion, and with the interviews I read from the director, there is a palpable frustration on how the movie has been taken, and I don't think it is a failure of the movie itself or the work of Takahata; I think it is a failure of humanity, which seeks the black-and-white perspective of everything that happens. Having strong stances is fine, such as being anti-zionist is something I consider to be important, but losing humanity and empathy is where the distortion occurs. This is why I am conflicted about the movie, as the message has been obscured over a simple and digestible "war is bad" idea.

Seita and Setsuko's relationship is the film's greatest beauty: a small world of tenderness and affection surrounded by hunger, cruelty and destruction. I understand its importance as a tribute to the countless children who became victims of war, but I remain somewhat unconvinced by its dramatic construction. A beautiful film that has already burned my heart. I don't want to watch it again. 6/10

Given its overwhelmingly positive reception and reputation as one of the most emotionally devastating animated films ever made, I went into Grave of the Fireflies with exceptionally high expectations. Unfortunately, despite its undeniably tragic subject matter, the film failed to resonate with me on the emotional level I had anticipated. I watched it with my wife, who had previously cried her eyes out watching Hachi: A Dog's Tale, yet neither of us felt particularly moved by this supposedly heartbreaking experience. Perhaps the animation style contributed to this emotional distance, but for whatever reason, we struggled to establish a genuine connection with the characters. On paper, the story is absolutely devastating, yet its emotional impact remained surprisingly limited for both of us. That being said, the film delivers a thoroughly respectable anti-war narrative, depicting the horrifying consequences of World War II for the civilian population, particularly innocent children. Its underlying message of compassion, humanity, and the importance of love over hatred is both meaningful and commendable. The contrast between childhood innocence and the merciless realities of war provides the story with an inherently powerful foundation. However, I found several aspects of the storytelling frustrating. Some of the young protagonist's decisions were difficult to comprehend, while the behavior of nearly every adult seemed unnecessarily irrational, at least from our contemporary perspective. Although these choices can certainly be interpreted within the historical and cultural circumstances of wartime Japan, they nevertheless made it increasingly difficult for us to sympathize with the characters and their predicament. The occasionally sluggish pacing further contributed to this sense of emotional detachment. Ultimately, the film's greatest weakness, at least for me, is that its devastating subject matter never translated into an equally devastating viewing experience. Without a sufficiently strong emotional connection to the protagonists, even the most tragic developments failed to leave the lasting impression I had expected.

There are certain films that completely bank on the idea that it has to "destroy" the viewer, and the entire purpose of the film is to make them cry. This isn't always a bad thing, but I find myself not completely engaging with some of those films. I was kind of scared going into this for that reason, and ended up having the complete opposite experience. This is incredibly made in every category which won me over almost immediately.  The ideas presented here are enough to tug on the heartstrings, but it's the way the filmmaking supports this that made it all work for me compared to some other films you could label as "emotion bait." It's a tight almost 90 minute film, but accomplishes so much in it's very purposeful script. The animation had me taken aback so many times, and my god that score is absolutely beautiful. My new favorite Ghibli, although I do need to watch more.

Prachtige film! Deze animefilm is gebaseerd op het leven van de director zelf. In de film heb je een broer en een jongere zus die opgroeien in in japan tijdens WO2. Wanneer hun moeder sterft aan de oorlog en hun vader in de oorlog vecht, is de broer volledig verantwoordelijk voor zen zusje. Zo volg je dan hun drama doorheen de film. Elk moment van vreugde in hun leven is een moeilijk moment aangezien de eerste scene liet zien hoe dramatisch de film zou eindigen. Buiten gewoon laten zien wat een kutleven ze hadden geeft de film toch ook nog veel motieven mee die niet direct opvallen. Zo zie je hoe ignorant mensen omgaan met andere mensen die het slechter dan hun hebben en hoe genormaliseerd dit egoisme is. Ook kan je je afvragen wie zijn fout het nu is dat zij zo een kutleven kregen en dan vind je eigenlijk geen zwart wit antwoord maar dat zo goed als iedereen wel een beetje schuld draagt wat ik een betere representatie vind van oorlog dan de goeie tegen de slechte. Al bij al een sad film die goed gemaakt is! Joka Ciao
